O1.t: Explain that we see objects when reflected light enters our eyes, and compare shiny and dull surfaces.

O2.t: Draw rays to show reflection in a mirror (equal angles), describe mirror images and explain how a periscope works.

O6.t: Explain day, night and years, and describe the phases of the Moon.

captions: Hello, light scientists!
This is lesson 6.1: reflection.
Light travels in straight lines from a light source, like the Sun or a lamp.
Most objects are not light sources. We see them because light bounces off them and travels into our eyes.
When light bounces off a surface, we call it reflection.
All surfaces reflect some light.
Smooth, shiny surfaces, like mirrors, reflect light very well in one direction.
Rough, dull surfaces scatter the light in many directions.
Pause and think. Why can we see a book, even though it does not give out its own light?
We draw light as straight lines with arrows, called rays.
The ray going towards the mirror is the incident ray. The ray bouncing off is the reflected ray.
The angle at which the light hits the mirror is equal to the angle at which it bounces off.
When you look in a plane mirror, you see an image of yourself.
The image is the same size as you, and it looks as far behind the mirror as you are in front.
But it is reversed. Raise your right hand, and your image raises its left!
Your turn. In a mirror, what do you notice about the two angles of the light rays?
A periscope lets you see over walls, using two mirrors.
Fix a mirror at each end of a long box, both tilted at forty-five degrees.
Light from an object reflects off the top mirror, down the tube,
and off the bottom mirror into your eye.
Let's remember.
Light travels in straight lines.
We see objects when light reflected from them enters our eyes.
In a mirror, the angles of the incident and reflected rays are equal.
And a periscope uses two mirrors.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, light scientists!
This is lesson 6.2: refraction.
Put a straw in a glass of water.
It looks broken where it goes into the water. But the straw is still straight!
This happens because light changes direction when it passes from water into air.
Light travels at different speeds in different materials, such as air, water and glass.
When light passes from one material into another at an angle, it bends.
This bending of light is called refraction.
Pause and think. What is the bending of light called?
A lens is a curved piece of glass or plastic that refracts light.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle. It bends light rays so they meet at a point called the focal point.
Magnifying glasses, glasses, cameras and even your eyes use lenses.
White light is a mixture of many colours.
A glass prism refracts each colour by a slightly different amount, so the colours spread out.
We see a band of colours called a spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
A rainbow forms when sunlight shines through raindrops.
Each drop refracts and reflects the light, and splits it into colours, like a tiny prism.
To see a rainbow, the Sun must be behind you, and the rain in front.
Your turn. What splits sunlight into colours to make a rainbow?
Try this trick.
Put a coin in an empty cup, and move your head back until you just cannot see the coin.
Keep still while a friend slowly pours water into the cup.
The coin appears! The water refracts the light from the coin towards your eyes.
Let's remember.
Refraction is the bending of light.
Light bends when it passes from one material into another.
A convex lens brings light rays together at a focal point.
And a prism splits white light into a spectrum of colours.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, space scientists!
This is lesson 6.3: the Solar System.
At the centre of our Solar System is a star: the Sun.
Eight planets travel around the Sun. Their paths are called orbits.
In order from the Sun, they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
A star, like the Sun, gives out its own light.
A planet orbits a star. It does not make light; it reflects light from the Sun.
A moon orbits a planet. The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite.
Pause and think. Which planet is closest to the Sun?
The Earth spins on its axis once every twenty-four hours. That gives us day and night.
The Earth orbits the Sun once every three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days. That is one year.
Planets further from the Sun take longer to go around it.
The Moon orbits the Earth about once every twenty-seven days.
Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, but as it moves around us, we see different amounts of the lit half.
These shapes are called phases: new moon, crescent, first quarter, gibbous and full moon.
As the lit part grows, the Moon is waxing. As it shrinks, the Moon is waning.
Your turn. What do we call it when the lit part of the Moon is getting bigger each night?
Become an astronomer!
Look at the Moon at the same time each clear night, and draw its shape.
Keep your Moon diary for four weeks.
You will see the whole cycle of phases, and it will start again.
Let's remember.
Eight planets orbit the Sun.
The Earth spins once a day, and orbits the Sun once a year.
The Moon orbits the Earth in about a month.
And we see the Moon's phases change.
Fantastic work, scientists! You have finished Stage 6 science lessons. See you in the practice room.

h.title: Moon diary
h.intro: Watch the Moon for four weeks and record how much of it is lit.
need: the table below or a notebook
an adult to go outside with you
safety: Go outside only with an adult.
steps: Once a week, look at the Moon at about the same time.
Estimate how much of the Moon is lit: 0% (new moon), 50% (half), 100% (full).
Write your estimate in the table. If it is cloudy, try the next clear night.
Look for the pattern: is the Moon waxing or waning?
